newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 26.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 26.

text.p: The Superannuation Accord was in tatters on Tuesday after the Coalition Government's decision to push ahead with a referendum on compulsory superannuation. Justice Minister Doug Graham said on Tuesday that a $10 million public referendum would be held in September but he did not issue details of the compulsory scheme to be voted on. Voting will be conducted between September 5 and 26, with results in early October. Page 1.

Tukoroirangi Morgan promised in his maiden speech on Tuesday that he would never again be caught with his pants down. Morgan, who has been under attack for spending thousands of dollars of Aotearoa Television Network money on clothing, including $89 underpants, briefly apologised for his mistakes. However, humility was not a big part of his speech. Page 1. ----

Prime Minister Jim Bolger failed on Tuesday to rule out futher state asset sales, prompting Labour to raise the spectre of a secret privatisation agenda that flouts the Coalition accord. NZ First leader and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters described his party's capitulation to National over plans to sell eight small power stations -- despite its pre-election opposition to asset privatisation -- as a compromise made in the interests of forming a government. Page 2.

The government was considering sending an airforce plane to check on a shipment of plutonium waste sailing to Japan through the Tasman sea, acting Foreign Affairs Minister Simon Upton said on Tuesday. He said he was told that at 1pm on Tuesday the ship was 647 kilometres east of Sydney, which meant it was well clear of New Zealand's exclusive economic zone. Page 2.

Problems with the education payroll were at crisis point and schools and teachers should be offered compensation, Labour associate education spokesman Steve Maharey said on Tuesday. Maharey used Parliament's question time to ask Education Minister Wyatt Creech what action he had taken and when staff who were owed money would be paid. Page 2.

Immigration officials have told the Coalition Government that implementing its immigration policy could harm tourism and international relations. The advice is contained in a paper on the implications of the coalition agreement signed by National and NZ First in December. "Health screening of overseas visitors" was one of the key initiatives. The agreement did not say where or by whom checks should be performed or whether some visitors would be exempt. Page 2.

Speaker Doug Kidd is considering ACT NZ's complaint about the colourful language Alliance MP Pam Corkery used in her maiden speech in Parliament last week. ACT NZ whip Ken Shirley and Alliance leader Jim Anderton said the complaint did not make it on to the agenda of Parliament's business committee meeting on Tuesday as it was judged a matter for the Speaker alone to consider. Page 2.

Feltex Carpets, New Zealand's largest wool carpet maker, intends to seek a listing on the Stock Exchange, though the company has given no time-table. Feltex Carpets was part of the giant Feltex Group, one of the top ten companies in New Zealand in the 1970s and 1980s. Feltex Carpets is one of the six largest wool carpet manufacturers in the world, and ranks in the top 50 carpet companies in the world for the manufacture of nylon and wool carpets. Page 14.

Jewellery has sparkled for Michael Hill International despite being an item of discretionary spending in a tight retailing period. The company reported on Tuesday a 5.7 percent lift in tax-paid profit till December 31 and is forecasting a full-year result of between $5.3 million and $5.5 million. Interim earnings of $4.37 million (up from $4.13 million in the same period of 1995) were a record for a six-month period. Page 14.

November quarterly employment survey wage data issued on Tuesday support a tightening of monetary policy sooner rather than later, economists said. Economists were concerned that wage pressures did not seem to be reducing, but noted that a Reserve Bank tightening was not imminent. They said there was a danger inflationary wage pressure could pick up this year. Page 14.

Credit rating agency Moody's Investors Service has confirmed its Aal long-term rating of Telecom Corporation debt. The agency's decision not to change its rating contrasted with a ratings downgrade for Telecom announced by a rival agency, Standard and Poor's, earlier this month. Both agencies reviewed Telecom after the company announced a $1 billion share buyback programme. Moody's agreed with the Standing and Poor's observation that the use of external financing for the buyback programme would reduce financial ratios, including the level of interest cover. Page 14.

The business outlook is "mildly positive" in the National Bank's latest survey of business opinion, but it says the results fall short of sustaining robust economic growth. A net 12 percent of businesses surveyed this month expect an improvement in conditions in the year ahead, up slightly on the net seven percent positive in December. Businesses are also subdued in their expectations about investment, profits and jobs. Page 14.

Justice secretary John Belgrave would become the director of the Electricity Supply Association, association chariman Doug Matheson said on Tuesday. Belgrave would replace former director Barrie Leay, who had resigned to explore business opportunities in the energy sector. The changeover was expected in June. Matheson said the association was pleased to have attracted "a wide range of candidates of the calibre of Mr Belgrave" for the position. Page 15.

Tower Corporation is still looking at the possibility of becoming a listed company. There has been continued speculation about "demutualisation" by Tower among other mutual life insurance groups after the listing of National Mutual. AMP shareholders will vote later this year whether to list on the stock exchange. Page 15.

Fletcher Challenge's first-half profit, due today, will reflect the big swings in commodity prices, fund managers and analysts predict. Analysts expect the company's pulp and paper division to report between a first-half net loss of $20 million and a net profit of $10 million. That is down from a $186 million profit in the same period a year earlier, reflecting a marked decline in pulp and paper. Page 16.
